title: Kyiv’s warnings of tens of thousands more North Korean troops never came true
gist: Despite repeated Ukrainian forecasts of 30,000-100,000 more North Korean troops, the deployment in Russia has plateaued at an estimated 14,000-16,000 (9,500 active) since late 2024. Vu attributes the pause to the war's shift away from Russian soil (the alliance treaty doesn't cover Ukraine), the move to long-range missile/drone warfare, and domestic control/defection risks — while Pyongyang has already banked combat experience, weapons showcasing, technology transfers and labourer hard currency.

insights.claim: Zelenskyy claimed in November 2024 that North Korea could send up to 100,000 troops, Ukraine anticipated another 30,000 in July 2025, and in August 2026 Zelenskyy revised his expectation to 50,000 — none of which eventuated.
insights.speaker: Khang Vu
insights.so_what: Discount Ukrainian escalation forecasts on North Korean deployments.
insights.quote: these larger troop deployments have never eventuated

insights.claim: Estimated North Korean troops in Russia remain between 14,000 and 16,000, up from the initial 12,000 in October 2024, with the discrepancy explained by differing estimation methods; North Korea has largely stopped sending troops since late 2024 and the South Korean military detects no signs of future deployment.
insights.speaker: Khang Vu
insights.so_what: Base case: no step-up in North Korean manpower for Russia.

insights.claim: Russia needs personnel and is expanding recruitment to Africa, yet there is no sign Moscow has asked North Korea for more troops.
insights.speaker: Khang Vu
insights.so_what: Russia's manpower constraint persists; watch African recruitment as substitute.
insights.locator: North Korea’s pause is worth noting.

insights.claim: The pause reflects the changing war: Ukraine's counteroffensive now focuses on recapturing territory in Donetsk Oblast and it has not attacked Russian territory since withdrawing from Kursk in March 2025, while North Korea's alliance treaty with Russia does not cover Ukraine, including Russian-occupied land.
insights.speaker: Khang Vu
insights.so_what: North Korean troop involvement is tied to threats on Russian soil — a renewed Ukrainian incursion into Russia would be the trigger to watch.
insights.quote: the scope of its alliance treaty with Russia doesn’t cover Ukraine

insights.claim: The shift to long-range missiles and drones striking deep behind the front reduces the value of North Korean troops, who offer little air defence capability.
insights.speaker: Khang Vu
insights.so_what: Russia's demand is for air defence and munitions rather than infantry.
insights.locator: Instead, the pause in North Korean

insights.claim: Domestic control concerns constrain Pyongyang: it hid the deployment, issued death certificates citing deaths 'in training', admitted casualties only in April 2025, and Ukraine's handover of two captured soldiers to South Korea highlighted defection risks.
insights.speaker: Khang Vu
insights.so_what: Regime-stability considerations cap the scale of North Korea's foreign military adventures.

insights.claim: No diplomatic breakthrough explains the pause: North Korea continues to reject dialogue with the United States and South Korea.

insights.claim: North Korea has already achieved its main objectives: real combat experience to teach at home, battlefield demonstration of its weapons to prospective buyers, and fulfilment of its alliance obligation in Kursk repaid by Russian sharing of sensitive military technology.
insights.speaker: Khang Vu
insights.so_what: Russian tech transfer to North Korea raises long-term regional security risk for South Korea and Japan; North Korean arms exports may grow.

insights.claim: North Korea will likely rely on the 9,500 active soldiers still in Russia to meet its defence obligations, and that number is not expected to rise anytime soon.
